stem: Zubaida, 67, slips in her courtyard and falls on her outstretched hand. Her wrist looks like a dinner fork from the side. X-ray shows a transverse fracture of the distal radius about 2 cm above the joint with dorsal displacement and dorsal angulation of the distal fragment. What is this fracture called?
explanation: A Colles fracture is an extra-articular distal radius fracture with dorsal displacement and angulation, typically in an osteoporotic woman after a fall on the outstretched hand, producing the dinner-fork deformity. A Smith fracture has volar displacement, usually after a fall on the flexed wrist.

stem: A 22-year-old cricketer falls on his outstretched hand. He has tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox and pain on axial compression of the thumb. Scaphoid-view X-rays show no fracture. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Crepe bandage and review if pain persists after 6 weeks
Immobilise in a splint and arrange MRI or repeat X-rays in 10–14 days
Immediate open reduction and internal fixation with a compression screw
explanation: Scaphoid fractures are often invisible on initial X-rays, so clinical suspicion is treated as a fracture with immobilisation and further imaging (MRI, CT or repeat films). A missed scaphoid fracture can progress to non-union or avascular necrosis of the proximal pole, so discharge without follow-up is unsafe.

stem: A 7-year-old boy falls from a tree onto his outstretched arm and sustains a displaced extension-type supracondylar fracture of the humerus. The hand is warm and pink. He cannot flex the tip of his thumb or index finger to make an 'OK' sign, but sensation in the hand is normal. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: The anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve supplies flexor pollicis longus and the lateral flexor digitorum profundus, so injury prevents the 'OK' sign with no sensory loss because the nerve is purely motor. It is the nerve most often injured in extension-type supracondylar fractures; radial nerve injury would cause weak wrist and finger extension.

stem: An 8-year-old with a displaced supracondylar fracture of the humerus has a cold, pale hand with no radial pulse before reduction. Which artery is most at risk in this injury?
explanation: The sharp proximal fragment of an extension supracondylar fracture is displaced anteriorly and can kink, compress or tear the brachial artery in the cubital fossa. Untreated ischaemia can lead to forearm compartment syndrome and Volkmann ischaemic contracture, so a pulseless hand needs urgent reduction.

stem: A 24-year-old kabaddi player falls on his abducted, externally rotated arm. His shoulder has lost its rounded contour and the humeral head is palpable in front. Before attempting reduction, sensation over which area must be tested and documented?
options: The tip of the little finger
The lateral aspect of the upper arm over the deltoid
The dorsal web space between the thumb and the index finger
The medial aspect of the forearm
explanation: Anterior shoulder dislocation can stretch the axillary nerve, which supplies the deltoid and the skin over its lower half (the regimental badge area). Sensation there is checked and recorded before and after reduction; the dorsal first web space is supplied by the radial nerve.

stem: A 30-year-old man is brought in after a generalised tonic-clonic seizure. He holds his right arm internally rotated and adducted and cannot externally rotate it. AP X-ray shows a symmetrical 'light bulb' appearance of the humeral head. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Posterior dislocation is classically caused by seizures or electric shock, when strong internal rotators overpower the external rotators; the arm is locked in internal rotation and the humeral head looks like a light bulb on AP view. It is easily missed on a single AP film, so a lateral or axillary view is needed.

stem: A 19-year-old falls off a motorbike onto his shoulder. X-ray shows a minimally displaced fracture of the middle third of the right clavicle. Skin is intact and the arm is neurovascularly normal. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Figure-of-eight bandage applied tightly for 12 weeks
explanation: Most minimally displaced midshaft clavicle fractures heal well with a broad arm sling, analgesia and early movement as pain allows. Surgery is reserved for open fractures, skin tenting, neurovascular injury or marked displacement and shortening.

stem: A 28-year-old man raises his forearm to block a stick blow. X-ray shows a fracture of the proximal third of the ulnar shaft. The radial head does not line up with the capitulum on the lateral view. What is this injury called?
explanation: A proximal ulnar fracture with dislocation of the radial head is a Monteggia injury; a line through the radial neck should always pass through the capitulum, and the elbow must be imaged with every forearm fracture. Galeazzi is the opposite pattern: a distal radial shaft fracture with distal radioulnar joint dislocation.

stem: A 3-year-old girl started crying and refused to use her left arm after her father pulled her up by the hand onto a bus. She holds the arm slightly flexed and pronated. There is no swelling or bruising. What is the most appropriate management?
options: X-ray of the elbow, then an above-elbow plaster cast
Supination and flexion of the forearm
explanation: A pulled elbow is subluxation of the radial head under the annular ligament after traction on the extended, pronated arm. It is reduced by supination and flexion or by hyperpronation, often with a click, and the child soon uses the arm again; X-rays are not needed with a typical history and normal examination.

stem: A 21-year-old man punched a wall in anger. The knuckle of his right little finger is depressed and the dorsum of the hand is swollen. Which bone is most likely fractured?
options: Shaft of the proximal phalanx of the little finger
explanation: Punching a hard object typically fractures the neck of the fifth metacarpal (boxer's fracture), giving a depressed knuckle. A wound over the knuckle from a punch to the mouth must be treated as a human bite; a fracture at the base of the first metacarpal is a Bennett fracture.

stem: A 78-year-old woman with osteoporosis falls and sustains a minimally displaced fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus. Neurovascular examination is normal. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Open reduction and locking plate fixation
Collar and cuff sling with early mobilisation
explanation: Most minimally displaced proximal humerus fractures in older people are treated in a sling with early gentle mobilisation to avoid stiffness. Surgery is considered for markedly displaced fractures, fracture-dislocations and some head-splitting injuries.

stem: A 35-year-old carpenter injures his hand. X-ray shows an intra-articular fracture at the base of the first metacarpal, with a small medial fragment staying attached and the shaft pulled proximally and radially. Which muscle mainly causes the displacement of the shaft?
explanation: In a Bennett fracture the small volar-ulnar fragment is held by the ligament while abductor pollicis longus, inserted into the base of the first metacarpal, pulls the shaft proximally and radially. This unstable intra-articular fracture usually needs fixation.

stem: Rehmat Bibi, 84, walks indoors only with a frame and has moderate dementia. After a fall her left leg is shortened and externally rotated. X-ray shows a displaced intracapsular fracture of the femoral neck. She is otherwise fit for surgery. What is the most appropriate operation?
explanation: Displaced intracapsular fractures disrupt the blood supply of the femoral head, so the head is replaced rather than fixed; hemiarthroplasty suits older patients with limited mobility or cognitive impairment. Total hip replacement is offered to fit, independently mobile patients, and screw fixation is used for undisplaced fractures.

stem: A 79-year-old man falls at home. X-ray shows a stable two-part intertrochanteric fracture of the right femur. What is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: Extracapsular fractures leave the blood supply of the femoral head intact, so the fracture is fixed; a sliding hip screw is standard for stable intertrochanteric fractures. Replacement is for displaced intracapsular fractures, and prolonged traction carries high risk of pressure sores, pneumonia and thrombosis.

stem: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head is a common complication of displaced intracapsular femoral neck fractures. Which artery provides most of the blood supply to the adult femoral head?
explanation: In adults the femoral head is supplied mainly by retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery that run along the neck, and these are torn in displaced intracapsular fractures. The artery of the ligamentum teres contributes little after childhood.

stem: A 32-year-old car passenger hits his knee against the dashboard in a collision on the motorway. His right leg is shortened, flexed, adducted and internally rotated at the hip. Which nerve is most at risk?
explanation: A dashboard injury drives the femoral head backwards, causing posterior hip dislocation with the limb flexed, adducted and internally rotated, and the sciatic nerve lying behind the joint can be stretched. Urgent reduction is needed to reduce the risk of avascular necrosis and nerve damage.

stem: A 23-year-old man with a closed femoral shaft fracture awaiting fixation becomes confused 36 hours after injury. RR is 30/min, SpO₂ 86 % on air, and there are petechiae over his chest, axillae and conjunctivae. Chest X-ray shows bilateral patchy shadowing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The triad of respiratory distress, neurological change and petechial rash 24–72 hours after a long-bone fracture is typical of fat embolism syndrome. Pulmonary embolism does not cause a petechial rash, and early fracture fixation reduces the risk of fat embolism.

stem: A 30-year-old man arrives at the emergency department with an open fracture of the tibial shaft after a motorbike accident. There is a 3 cm wound with bone visible. He is haemodynamically stable. Apart from analgesia, splinting and tetanus cover, which step should be done first in the emergency department?
options: Primary closure of the wound in the emergency department
Intravenous antibiotics as soon as possible
Immediate internal fixation in the emergency department
Wound swab culture before giving any antibiotic
explanation: In open fractures, early intravenous antibiotics, ideally within an hour, are the most important measure to reduce deep infection, along with photographing and covering the wound with a saline dressing. Formal debridement and stabilisation follow in theatre; primary closure in the emergency room and swab-guided delay are harmful.

stem: A 26-year-old woman twists her ankle walking on an uneven pavement. She has swelling over the lateral ankle. According to the Ottawa ankle rules, which finding means she needs an ankle X-ray?
options: Marked swelling and pain below the lateral malleolus on standing
Pain on inversion of the foot
Bone tenderness at the posterior edge of the lateral malleolus
explanation: Ankle X-ray is indicated if there is malleolar pain with bone tenderness along the posterior edge or tip of either malleolus, or inability to bear weight for four steps both immediately and in the department. Swelling and bruising alone are common in ligament sprains and do not mandate imaging.

stem: A 40-year-old woman has an ankle injury. X-ray shows a fracture of the fibula above the syndesmosis with widening of the medial clear space, indicating talar shift. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Compression bandage and early weight bearing
explanation: A Weber C fibular fracture with talar shift is unstable because the syndesmosis and medial structures are disrupted; open reduction and internal fixation restores the mortise and prevents early arthritis. Cast or brace treatment is for stable injuries without talar shift.

stem: A 22-year-old footballer lands awkwardly while pivoting and feels a 'pop' in his knee. The knee swells within 1 hour. A few days later, the tibia moves forward excessively on the femur with the knee flexed 20–30°. What is the most likely injury?
explanation: A non-contact pivoting injury with a pop, rapid haemarthrosis and a positive Lachman test is typical of an anterior cruciate ligament tear. Meniscal tears usually swell more slowly, over hours to a day, and cause locking or joint-line tenderness.

stem: A 35-year-old man twisted his knee while squatting. The knee swelled the next day and he now has medial joint-line tenderness and episodes when the knee 'locks' and he cannot fully straighten it. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Twisting on a flexed knee, delayed swelling, joint-line tenderness and true locking point to a meniscal tear, with a displaced fragment blocking extension. A medial collateral ligament sprain causes tenderness along the ligament and pain on valgus stress, but not locking.

stem: A 45-year-old man playing badminton feels as if someone kicked the back of his ankle. He can walk with a limp. Lying prone, squeezing his calf does not cause plantarflexion of the foot, and a gap is felt above the heel. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A sudden 'kick' sensation, a palpable gap and absent plantarflexion on calf squeeze (Simmonds or Thompson test) indicate Achilles tendon rupture. Patients may still walk and weakly plantarflex using the long toe flexors, so this is easily missed.

stem: Usman, an overweight 13-year-old boy, has had a limp and left knee pain for 4 weeks. Knee examination is normal. Hip flexion is accompanied by obligatory external rotation and internal rotation is reduced. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Transient synovitis of the hip joint
explanation: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis typically affects overweight adolescents, may present with referred knee pain, and causes loss of internal rotation with external rotation on flexion; a frog-leg lateral X-ray shows the slip. Perthes disease affects younger children, usually 4–8 years old.

stem: A 25-year-old man had a closed tibial shaft fracture treated in an above-knee plaster 8 hours ago. He now has severe pain not relieved by morphine and pain when his toes are passively extended. Foot pulses are palpable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Pain out of proportion to the injury and pain on passive stretch of the muscles are the earliest signs of compartment syndrome. Pulses usually remain present because compartment pressure rarely exceeds arterial pressure, so a palpable pulse does not exclude it.

stem: A 28-year-old man with a tibial fracture in a full plaster cast has increasing leg pain and pain on passive toe movement. The cast and padding are split down to the skin and the leg is placed at heart level, but 30 minutes later his pain and signs are unchanged. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Elevate the leg above heart level and give more opioid
Emergency fasciotomy of all four leg compartments
Doppler ultrasound of the leg veins
explanation: Clinical compartment syndrome that persists after all dressings are released down to skin requires urgent fasciotomy of all compartments to prevent muscle and nerve necrosis. Elevation above heart level reduces arterial inflow and worsens perfusion, and waiting allows irreversible damage.

stem: Junior doctors on an orthopaedic ward in Multan are taught to look for compartment syndrome after forearm and leg fractures. Which is the earliest and most reliable clinical sign?
options: Absent distal pulses on palpation and on Doppler examination
Pain on passive stretch of the compartment muscles
explanation: Pain out of proportion to the injury and pain on passive stretch are the earliest signs of raised compartment pressure. Pulselessness, pallor and paralysis are late findings that indicate established ischaemia, and waiting for them leads to permanent damage.

stem: A sedated, ventilated 35-year-old with a tibial plateau fracture cannot report pain. Compartment pressures are measured. His diastolic BP is 60 mmHg and the anterior compartment pressure is 42 mmHg. What is the best interpretation?
options: Normal compartment pressure; repeat the measurement in 12 hours
A perfusion gradient of 18 mmHg indicates the need for fasciotomy
Compartment syndrome only if pressure exceeds diastolic pressure
Raised pressure but fasciotomy is only needed if pulses are lost
explanation: A perfusion gradient (diastolic pressure minus compartment pressure) below 30 mmHg indicates inadequate tissue perfusion and is the usual threshold for fasciotomy. Waiting for loss of pulses or for compartment pressure to exceed diastolic pressure would allow muscle necrosis.

stem: A 40-year-old man was trapped under a collapsed wall in an earthquake for 10 hours. After release his right thigh and leg are tense and swollen. His urine is dark brown, dipstick positive for blood, but microscopy shows no red cells. CK is 45,000 U/L. Which immediate treatment best protects his kidneys?
options: Intravenous furosemide to force a high urine output
explanation: Crush injury causes rhabdomyolysis, and myoglobin produces dark urine positive for blood on dipstick without red cells; aggressive intravenous isotonic fluid to maintain high urine output reduces myoglobin-induced acute kidney injury. Furosemide may worsen hypovolaemia, and dialysis is used only for refractory AKI, hyperkalaemia or overload.

stem: Ali, a 6-year-old boy, has had fever and severe pain above the right knee for 3 days and refuses to walk. The distal femur is warm and very tender. CRP is high. Which organism is the most likely cause?
explanation: Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest cause of acute haematogenous osteomyelitis at all ages, typically affecting the metaphysis of long bones in children. Pseudomonas is linked to puncture wounds through shoes, and Salmonella is classically associated with sickle cell disease.

stem: A 9-year-old boy with sickle cell anaemia has fever and pain in the left tibia for a week, not improving with treatment for a vaso-occlusive crisis. MRI confirms osteomyelitis. Besides Staphylococcus aureus, which organism must the empirical antibiotics cover?
explanation: Patients with sickle cell disease are particularly prone to Salmonella osteomyelitis, related to bowel infarcts allowing bacterial entry and to splenic dysfunction. Empirical therapy should therefore cover Salmonella as well as S. aureus, for example with a third-generation cephalosporin.

stem: Acute haematogenous osteomyelitis in children usually starts in the metaphysis of long bones. What explains this site?
options: Slow, turbulent flow in metaphyseal capillary loops
The epiphysis has an end-arterial supply from the joint capsule
The diaphysis has the richest blood supply
explanation: Metaphyseal capillaries form hairpin loops with slow, turbulent flow and few phagocytes, so circulating bacteria settle there. The growth plate then acts as a barrier that limits spread into the epiphysis in older children.

stem: Sana, a 4-year-old girl, has had fever of 39.2 °C and refused to bear weight on her right leg for 2 days. She holds the hip flexed, abducted and externally rotated, and any movement is very painful. WBC is 18,000/mm³ and CRP 110 mg/L. Ultrasound shows a hip effusion. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Oral ibuprofen and review in 48 hours
Urgent aspiration of the hip joint
MRI of the pelvis under sedation
explanation: Fever, inability to bear weight, high WBC and CRP and an effusion make septic arthritis likely, so the hip is aspirated urgently for Gram stain and culture, followed by washout and intravenous antibiotics. Pus in a joint quickly destroys cartilage and can cause avascular necrosis of the femoral head, so delay for observation or MRI is unsafe.

stem: A 30-year-old man has had a discharging sinus over his left tibia for 2 years after an open fracture. X-ray shows a dense, separated fragment of bone surrounded by a lucent zone and a shell of new periosteal bone. What is the definitive treatment?
options: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy with long-term antibiotics
Removal of dead bone, debridement and antibiotics
explanation: Chronic osteomyelitis with a sequestrum (a separated fragment of dead bone) cannot be cured by antibiotics alone because dead bone has no blood supply; sequestrectomy and debridement with targeted antibiotics are needed. Amputation is a last resort for uncontrollable infection or a non-functional limb.

stem: A 14-year-old boy has had a dull ache in the upper tibia for 3 months, worse at night. He is afebrile and inflammatory markers are mildly raised. X-ray shows a well-defined lucent lesion in the proximal tibial metaphysis with a thick sclerotic rim. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A Brodie abscess is a localised subacute osteomyelitis in which host defences wall off the infection, producing a metaphyseal lucency with a sclerotic rim and chronic pain without systemic upset. Osteosarcoma and Ewing sarcoma show aggressive, poorly defined destruction with periosteal reaction.

stem: Shazia, 32, from rural Punjab has had back pain for 4 months with evening fever and weight loss. There is a small angular kyphosis at the thoracolumbar junction. X-ray shows destruction of the adjacent margins of T12 and L1 with loss of the disc space between them and a fusiform paravertebral shadow. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Constitutional symptoms with a gibbus and destruction of two adjacent vertebrae with loss of the intervening disc and a paravertebral abscess are typical of spinal tuberculosis (Pott disease). Metastases usually destroy the pedicles and vertebral bodies but spare the disc space.

stem: A 55-year-old diabetic man has a hot, swollen, painful right knee with fever for 2 days. Knee aspiration yields turbid fluid with 85,000 white cells/mm³, mostly neutrophils, and Gram-positive cocci in clusters. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Rest, NSAIDs and repeat aspiration in 1 week
explanation: Purulent synovial fluid with Gram-positive cocci in clusters indicates staphylococcal septic arthritis, treated by drainage (arthroscopic or open washout, or repeated aspiration) plus intravenous antibiotics. Steroid injection into an infected joint is dangerous, and colchicine treats gout, which shows crystals rather than bacteria.

stem: A 15-year-old boy has had increasing pain and swelling above the left knee for 2 months, waking him at night. X-ray of the distal femoral metaphysis shows a destructive lesion with a 'sunburst' periosteal reaction and a Codman triangle. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Osteosarcoma is the commonest primary malignant bone tumour in adolescents, usually around the knee in the metaphysis, with sunburst spiculation and a Codman triangle from lifted periosteum. Ewing sarcoma tends to affect the diaphysis and gives an onion-skin periosteal reaction.

stem: A 12-year-old girl has a painful swelling in the middle of her right femur, intermittent fever and a raised ESR. X-ray shows a permeative lesion in the diaphysis with a layered 'onion-skin' periosteal reaction. Biopsy shows sheets of small round blue cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Ewing sarcoma affects children and adolescents, involves the diaphysis, gives an onion-skin periosteal reaction and is composed of small round blue cells; fever and raised ESR can mimic infection. Osteomyelitis is in the differential, but biopsy showing small round blue cells settles the diagnosis.

stem: A 30-year-old woman has a painful swelling at the knee. X-ray shows an eccentric, expansile lytic lesion with a 'soap-bubble' appearance in the distal femoral epiphysis, extending to the subchondral bone. Her growth plates are closed. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Giant cell tumour typically occurs after skeletal maturity, in the epiphysis of a long bone around the knee, as an eccentric expansile lytic lesion reaching the subchondral bone. Aneurysmal bone cysts and simple bone cysts usually occur in the metaphysis of younger patients.

stem: A 19-year-old man has had pain in his left thigh for 6 months, worse at night and relieved promptly by NSAIDs. CT shows a small lucent nidus under 1.5 cm in the femoral cortex surrounded by dense sclerosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Osteoid osteoma is a benign tumour of young people producing prostaglandins that cause night pain relieved by NSAIDs; imaging shows a small nidus with surrounding reactive sclerosis. It is commonly treated by radiofrequency ablation if symptoms persist.

stem: A 16-year-old boy has a painless hard lump near his knee that has been present for years. X-ray shows a bony projection from the metaphysis of the distal femur pointing away from the joint, with its cortex and medulla continuous with the parent bone. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Osteochondroma, the commonest benign bone tumour, is a cartilage-capped bony outgrowth from the metaphysis that points away from the joint and shares cortex and medulla with the parent bone. Enchondromas lie within the medulla, often in the small bones of the hand.

stem: A 66-year-old man has back pain, anaemia, raised creatinine and multiple 'punched-out' lytic lesions in the skull on X-ray. Serum protein electrophoresis shows a monoclonal band. Which investigation is least sensitive for detecting his bone lesions?
explanation: Myeloma lesions are purely lytic with little osteoblastic activity, so isotope bone scans are often normal ('cold'). Whole-body low-dose CT and MRI are the most sensitive, and a skeletal survey still detects established lytic lesions.

stem: A 55-year-old woman with known breast cancer has pain in the right thigh on walking. X-ray shows a lytic metastasis in the subtrochanteric femur destroying more than half of the cortical thickness. There is no fracture. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Prophylactic intramedullary nailing followed by radiotherapy
Radiotherapy alone with full weight bearing as tolerated
Bisphosphonate infusion and review in 3 months
explanation: A painful lytic lesion with more than 50 % cortical destruction in the high-stress peritrochanteric region has a high risk of pathological fracture, so prophylactic fixation is followed by radiotherapy to the whole bone. Radiotherapy alone does not restore strength quickly enough to prevent fracture.

stem: Saleem, 38, a porter, has low back pain radiating down the back of his left thigh and calf to the sole and lateral border of the foot. The left ankle reflex is absent and plantarflexion is weak. Which nerve root is most likely compressed?
explanation: S1 root compression, usually from an L5/S1 disc prolapse, causes pain and numbness along the back of the leg to the sole and lateral foot, weak plantarflexion and a reduced ankle reflex. L5 compression weakens great toe extension and ankle dorsiflexion with numbness over the dorsum of the foot, and the reflexes are usually preserved.

stem: A 42-year-old woman has sciatica with numbness over the dorsum of the right foot and first web space. She has weakness of great toe extension; knee and ankle reflexes are normal. Which disc prolapse most likely explains this?
explanation: Weak extensor hallucis longus and numbness over the dorsum of the foot indicate an L5 root lesion, usually caused by a posterolateral L4/L5 disc prolapse compressing the traversing L5 root. An L5/S1 prolapse typically affects S1, reducing the ankle reflex.

stem: A 45-year-old man with a 2-week history of sciatica now has pain down both legs, numbness around the anus and perineum, and has not passed urine for 12 hours. Anal tone is reduced. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Urgent MRI of the lumbosacral spine
Plain X-ray of the lumbar spine
Physiotherapy referral and analgesia review in one week
explanation: Bilateral sciatica, saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention and reduced anal tone indicate cauda equina syndrome, which needs emergency MRI and surgical decompression to preserve bladder, bowel and sexual function. Plain X-rays do not show disc or neural compression.

stem: A 33-year-old office worker has had low back pain for 5 days after lifting a heavy box. There is no leg pain, numbness, bladder symptoms, fever, weight loss or history of cancer. Neurological examination is normal. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Strict bed rest on a firm mattress for 2 weeks
Advice to stay active with NSAIDs as needed
explanation: Acute non-specific low back pain without red flags is managed with reassurance, advice to keep active and simple analgesia such as an NSAID. Imaging does not change management and may find incidental changes, and bed rest delays recovery.

stem: A 28-year-old woman wearing only a lap belt is in a head-on car crash. She has a bruise across her lower abdomen and back pain. CT shows a horizontal fracture through the body, pedicles and spinous process of L1 (a flexion-distraction injury). Which associated injury must be actively looked for?
explanation: A Chance (flexion-distraction) fracture from a lap belt is strongly associated with hollow viscus injury, especially of the small bowel and mesentery, which CT can miss early. Calcaneal fractures are linked with lumbar burst fractures from falls onto the feet, not seat-belt injuries.

stem: A 74-year-old man with cervical spondylosis falls forward and hits his forehead, hyperextending his neck. He has marked weakness of both arms and hands, with milder weakness of the legs, and can still pass urine. CT shows no fracture. Which spinal cord syndrome is most likely?
explanation: Hyperextension in an older person with a narrowed spondylotic canal compresses the central cord, where the arm fibres of the corticospinal tracts lie medially, so the arms are weaker than the legs. Anterior cord syndrome causes paralysis and loss of pain sensation below the lesion with preserved proprioception.

stem: A 72-year-old woman falls down three stairs at home and complains of neck pain. She has no neurological deficit. By the Canadian C-spine rule she is high risk because of her age. Which imaging is most appropriate?
options: Three-view plain X-rays of the cervical spine
No imaging if she can rotate her neck 45°
explanation: Adults at high risk of cervical spine injury, including those aged 65 or over, should have CT of the cervical spine, which is far more sensitive than plain films for fractures. The rotation test is only applied to low-risk patients, and flexion-extension views are unsafe in the acute setting.

stem: During a school health check in Islamabad, a 13-year-old girl is noted to have uneven shoulders. Which bedside test best screens for structural scoliosis?
explanation: In the Adams forward bending test, vertebral rotation in structural scoliosis produces a rib hump that becomes obvious when the child bends forward. The Schober test measures lumbar flexion, used in ankylosing spondylitis, and straight leg raising tests for nerve root tension.

stem: A 35-year-old man falls from a motorcycle and sustains a spiral fracture of the middle third of the humeral shaft. He cannot extend his wrist or fingers and has numbness over the dorsum of the first web space. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: The radial nerve winds around the humerus in the spiral groove and is commonly injured by midshaft fractures, causing wrist drop and numbness over the dorsal first web space. Most cases are neurapraxia and recover with conservative treatment of the fracture.

stem: Farah, 30, is 32 weeks pregnant and has tingling of the thumb, index and middle fingers that wakes her at night. Shaking her hand relieves it. Tinel and Phalen tests are positive and there is no muscle wasting. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Night-time wrist splint in a neutral position
Nerve conduction studies before any treatment
explanation: Carpal tunnel syndrome in pregnancy is caused by fluid retention and usually resolves after delivery, so a neutral wrist splint at night is first-line. Surgery is reserved for persistent or severe cases with wasting or weakness, and nerve studies are not needed before conservative treatment of a typical case.

stem: A 25-year-old man has a fracture of the medial epicondyle of the humerus. When asked to grip a sheet of paper between his thumb and the side of his index finger, he flexes the thumb at the interphalangeal joint. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Froment's sign shows weakness of adductor pollicis, supplied by the ulnar nerve, so the patient substitutes flexor pollicis longus (median nerve) and flexes the thumb tip. The ulnar nerve runs behind the medial epicondyle and is easily injured there.

stem: A baby boy weighing 4.6 kg is delivered with shoulder dystocia at a THQ hospital. His right arm hangs by his side, adducted and internally rotated, with the elbow extended and the forearm pronated. The grasp reflex is present. Which roots are injured?
explanation: Erb palsy results from traction injury to the upper trunk (C5–C6), paralysing the shoulder abductors, external rotators, elbow flexors and supinators, giving the 'waiter's tip' posture with a preserved grasp. Lower root injury (C8–T1, Klumpke palsy) affects the small muscles of the hand.

stem: A 20-year-old man grabbed a railing to stop a fall from a height, forcibly abducting his arm. He now has a claw hand with wasting of the small hand muscles, numbness along the inner forearm, and on the same side a small pupil and drooping eyelid. Which injury is most likely?
options: Upper trunk lesion of the brachial plexus
Lower trunk lesion with avulsion of the T1 root
Ulnar nerve injury at the elbow
Radial nerve injury in the axilla
explanation: Forced abduction injures the lower trunk (C8–T1), causing Klumpke palsy with weakness of the intrinsic hand muscles and medial forearm numbness. An ipsilateral Horner syndrome indicates T1 root avulsion close to the cord, damaging sympathetic fibres to the eye and suggesting a poor prognosis.

stem: A 40-year-old man has a fracture of the neck of the fibula after a side impact to the knee. He walks with a high-stepping gait and cannot dorsiflex or evert his foot. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: The common peroneal (fibular) nerve winds around the neck of the fibula, where fractures or tight plasters can injure it, causing foot drop with loss of dorsiflexion and eversion. Tibial nerve injury weakens plantarflexion and inversion and causes numbness of the sole.

stem: A 50-year-old woman has a mastectomy with axillary node clearance. Afterwards the medial border of her scapula sticks out when she pushes against a wall. Which nerve has been damaged?
explanation: The long thoracic nerve runs on the medial wall of the axilla and supplies serratus anterior, which holds the scapula against the chest wall; damage causes winging of the scapula. The thoracodorsal nerve supplies latissimus dorsi, whose loss weakens adduction and extension rather than causing winging.

stem: After a long operation with an upper-arm tourniquet, a 30-year-old man has weakness of wrist extension and patchy numbness. Nerve conduction shows a block at the tourniquet site with normal conduction distal to it. He recovers fully within 4 weeks. What type of nerve injury was this?
explanation: Neurapraxia is a local conduction block, often from compression, with intact axons, so there is no Wallerian degeneration and recovery is complete within weeks. Axonotmesis involves axonal disruption with distal degeneration and recovery by regrowth at about 1 mm per day.

stem: A 24-year-old man had a scaphoid fracture through the waist treated in a cast. Six months later he still has wrist pain. MRI shows the proximal pole is dense with low signal. What is the most likely complication?
options: Avascular necrosis of the proximal pole
explanation: The scaphoid's blood supply enters distally and flows retrograde, so fractures through the waist or proximal pole can deprive the proximal fragment of blood, causing avascular necrosis and non-union. Malunion of the scaphoid is less common and does not produce a dead proximal pole.

stem: A 30-year-old man falls on his hand. X-ray shows a fracture of the distal third of the radial shaft with the ulnar head dislocated at the wrist. What is this injury called?
explanation: A Galeazzi injury is a distal radial shaft fracture with dislocation of the distal radioulnar joint, and in adults it needs open reduction and fixation. Monteggia is the reverse pattern, with a proximal ulnar fracture and radial head dislocation.

stem: A 60-year-old woman falls backwards onto the back of her flexed wrist. X-ray shows a transverse fracture of the distal radius with the distal fragment displaced and angled towards the palm. What is this fracture called?
explanation: A Smith fracture is a distal radius fracture with volar displacement of the distal fragment, often called a reverse Colles fracture, and is usually unstable. A Colles fracture has dorsal displacement after a fall on the outstretched hand.

stem: At her 6-week check, a firstborn girl delivered by breech has a clunk when the flexed and abducted hip is lifted forward (Ortolani test). Which investigation is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis?
explanation: In infants under about 4–6 months the femoral heads are largely cartilaginous, so ultrasound is the investigation of choice for developmental dysplasia of the hip. Plain X-rays become useful once the femoral head ossific nucleus appears.

stem: A 6-year-old boy has had a painless limp for 2 months. He is afebrile, with limited abduction and internal rotation of the right hip. X-ray shows a flattened, sclerotic and fragmented right femoral capital epiphysis. What is the underlying process?
options: Slipped epiphysis at the growth plate
Bacterial infection of the hip joint
Idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head
Inflammatory synovitis after a viral infection
explanation: Perthes disease is idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral capital epiphysis in children, usually boys aged 4–8, presenting with a painless or mildly painful limp and X-ray sclerosis, fragmentation and flattening. Slipped capital femoral epiphysis affects older, often overweight adolescents.

stem: A 13-year-old boy who plays football daily has pain below the right kneecap that is worse after running and kneeling. There is a tender bony lump over the tibial tuberosity. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Osgood–Schlatter disease is a traction apophysitis of the tibial tuberosity in active adolescents during growth spurts, causing a tender bony lump, and it settles with activity modification. Osteosarcoma causes progressive, constant and night pain rather than activity-related pain over the tuberosity.

stem: A 10-year-old boy had an untreated supracondylar fracture with a pulseless hand 6 months ago. He now has a fixed flexion deformity of the wrist and fingers that worsens when the wrist is extended. Which muscle group is mainly involved?
options: Deep flexor muscles of the forearm
explanation: Volkmann ischaemic contracture follows untreated forearm compartment syndrome, most often affecting the deep flexors (flexor digitorum profundus and flexor pollicis longus), which become fibrotic and shortened. The deformity worsens when the wrist is extended because the shortened flexors are stretched.

stem: A nurse asks which finding in suspected compartment syndrome of the leg is a late sign, indicating that ischaemic damage is already advanced. Which is it?
options: Pain out of proportion to the injury
explanation: Loss of distal pulses occurs late, if at all, because compartment pressure rarely exceeds arterial pressure; by then muscle necrosis is usually established. Pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch are the early warning signs that should prompt action.

stem: A 5-year-old boy has had a limp and mild right hip pain for 2 days after a cold last week. He is afebrile, bears some weight, and has mildly reduced internal rotation. WBC and CRP are normal. Ultrasound shows a small hip effusion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Transient synovitis follows a viral infection in young children, causes a limp with mild pain and a small effusion, and the child is afebrile with normal inflammatory markers. Septic arthritis is suggested by fever, refusal to bear weight, raised WBC and high CRP.

stem: A 25-year-old man from Quetta has 6 weeks of mid-back pain, night sweats and weight loss. Chest X-ray shows old apical scarring. Which is the earliest radiographic change expected in early tuberculous spondylitis?
options: Narrowing of the disc space with paradiscal erosion
explanation: Spinal tuberculosis usually begins in the paradiscal region, and the earliest X-ray signs are narrowing of the disc space and erosion of adjacent vertebral margins; collapse and gibbus come later. A bamboo spine is a feature of ankylosing spondylitis.

stem: A 42-year-old man has had a known bony lump on his upper humerus since childhood. It has started to enlarge and become painful over 6 months. MRI shows a cartilage cap 3 cm thick. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Growth or new pain in an osteochondroma after skeletal maturity, especially with a cartilage cap thicker than about 2 cm, suggests malignant change to chondrosarcoma. Overlying bursitis can cause pain but does not thicken the cartilage cap.

stem: A 50-year-old man has dull pain in the left hip and buttock for a year. X-ray shows a lytic lesion in the ilium with stippled 'rings and arcs' calcification and cortical thickening. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Chondrosarcoma typically affects middle-aged and older adults in the pelvis and proximal long bones, with a chondroid matrix showing rings-and-arcs calcification. Osteosarcoma and Ewing sarcoma are mainly tumours of children and adolescents.

stem: Among patients presenting to a GP clinic with low back pain, which feature most strongly calls for urgent imaging to exclude spinal metastasis?
options: Pain after lifting a heavy object
Previous breast cancer with constant night pain
explanation: A history of cancer, together with constant or night pain, is a red flag for spinal metastasis and calls for urgent MRI. Pain after lifting or prolonged sitting fits mechanical back pain, and brief morning stiffness is common in non-specific back pain.

stem: A 50-year-old man has pain from the front of the thigh to the medial side of the leg, weak knee extension and a reduced knee reflex. Which nerve root is most likely compressed?
explanation: L4 root compression causes pain over the anterior thigh and medial leg, weak quadriceps and a reduced knee reflex. An L5 lesion spares the knee reflex and weakens great toe extension, and S1 reduces the ankle reflex.

stem: A 25-year-old man is stabbed in the back on the right side at the T10 level. He has weakness of the right leg and loss of vibration and joint position sense in the right leg. Which other finding is expected?
options: Loss of pain and temperature sensation in the left leg
Loss of pain and temperature sensation in the right leg
Loss of all sensation in both legs
explanation: Brown-Séquard syndrome (hemisection of the cord) causes ipsilateral motor weakness and loss of dorsal column sensation, with contralateral loss of pain and temperature because the spinothalamic fibres cross within one or two segments of entry. The opposite leg keeps its power.

stem: A 45-year-old obese man who has recently started wearing a tight work belt has burning pain and numbness over the outer front of the right thigh. Power and reflexes are normal. Which nerve is compressed?
options: Lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh
explanation: Meralgia paraesthetica is entrapment of the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh as it passes under or through the inguinal ligament near the anterior superior iliac spine, causing purely sensory symptoms on the anterolateral thigh. An L3 or femoral nerve lesion would reduce knee reflex or power.

stem: After fixation of a radial head fracture, a 35-year-old woman cannot extend her fingers at the metacarpophalangeal joints, but she can extend her wrist (with radial deviation) and has no sensory loss. Which nerve is injured?
options: Radial nerve in the spiral groove
explanation: The posterior interosseous nerve is the deep motor branch of the radial nerve around the radial neck; injury causes finger drop without wrist drop or sensory loss, and the wrist deviates radially because extensor carpi radialis longus is spared. A spiral groove lesion causes wrist drop with numbness over the first dorsal web space.

stem: A 6-year-old boy develops foot drop and numbness of the sole after an intramuscular injection given into the lower inner part of the buttock at a private clinic. To avoid this injury, where should a gluteal intramuscular injection be given?
options: Lower inner quadrant of the buttock
Lower outer quadrant of the buttock
Upper outer quadrant of the buttock
explanation: The sciatic nerve passes through the lower inner part of the buttock, so injections there can damage it and cause foot drop and sensory loss. The upper outer quadrant (or, preferably, the ventrogluteal site or the anterolateral thigh in children) avoids the nerve.
